about: Constraint cards for the idea engine. One is drawn per film; the concept must obey it. A constraint forces the film off the expected path. Add cards when a film shows a new way to break habit (crew job 9).
cards: The host never speaks to camera: the story is told by what the cast does.
Everything in the film is made of one material (paper, glass, clay, light, pixels, chalk).
One colour only, plus black and white.
The camera never cuts: one continuous journey through several worlds.
The film starts at the ending and works backwards.
The viewer's own screen is a character: notifications, a cursor, a search bar.
Scale is the story: start microscopic, end at the size of a planet (or the reverse).
Every world change happens through an object the cast touches.
The sidekick is the hero; the host only reacts.
The text is the floor, the walls and the props: the cast walks on words.
Time of day changes with every beat, from dawn to night.
A rival character tries to make the opposite point and loses on screen.
The film looks like a game: a HUD, a level bar, a boss at the end.
Nothing is shown straight on: every shot is a reflection, a screen, a window or a shadow.
Each beat is a different art style, joined by one moving object.
Gravity is wrong: things fall up, sideways, or not at all.
The film is a heist: a plan, a team, a twist.
The ending pays off a background detail planted in the first three seconds.
Only three shots, each one long and moving through a lot of space.
The numbers are physical objects the cast carries, stacks and breaks.
The narrator is wrong at first and the picture corrects them.
It all happens inside one object (a phone, a coffee cup, a monitor, a book).
Silence beat: two seconds with no words in the middle of the film, carried by picture and sound.
The film borrows the grammar of a genre that has nothing to do with the topic (nature documentary, sports replay, cooking show, horror trailer).
Every shot has the camera moving in the same direction, like a single slide across a mural.
The cast is tiny in a giant world for the whole film until the last shot flips the scale.
One impossible moment every ten seconds.
The call to action is built physically in the world, not typed on top.
A split screen of two worlds that merge by the end.
The film is a countdown: every beat removes one thing until one remains.
